summary: Customer wants to validate private/VPC deployment for regulated biotech workloads. Main concerns: strict egress control, BYOK/KMS integration + HSM, audit log retention and SIEM integration, RBAC/SSO, and SOC 2 evidence. Discussed architecture patterns (private endpoints, NAT vs egress gateway, transit gateway peering), encryption in transit/rest, and hardened bastion/jump host strategy. Agreed next steps: share artifacts, pilot with locked-down egress and KMS BYOK, follow-up deep dive on SIEM ingestion.
transcript:
Meeting header
15:00 UTC · 2025-09-30 · 58 mins
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reyes (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM); Dr. Emily Carter (CTO), Liam O'Connor (Head Infra), Sana Ahmed (Security Eng), Tomislav Novak (DevOps)

Summary (auto): Quick run through of Solaris' security constraints and a proposed private deployment architecture. Action items captured.

00:00 Speaker 1: okay everyone we'll get started in a minute, thanks for joining
00:08 Maya Patel: hey all, Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE, with me is Jonah our solutions engineer and Priya on customer success. thanks for sharing time today
00:16 Dr. Emily Carter: thanks Maya, we wanted to do a session that's very focused on network hardening, egress, and the SOC 2 evidence we'll need for our clinical analytics workloads
00:25 Jonah Reyes: great, emily, can you run us through the top three blockers for you right now? is it egress, key management, or auditability mostly?
00:33 Liam O'Connor: it's a mix. egress is the top one — our compliance team requires that only a small set of IPs and FQDNs can be contacted from the VPC. second is BYOK, we need to control keys via our HSM. third is log forwarding to our SIEM (we use Splunk on-prem) with strict retention reqs
00:50 Sana Ahmed: and to add, RBAC needs to map to our SSO (Okta) with least privilege. we also have to document in SOC 2 how we restrict network egress and who can rotate keys
01:05 Jonah Reyes: makes sense. At a high level Redwood Private offers a VPC deployment where the control plane can be customer-managed and you can pin all outbound egress to an egress gateway or NAT bound to specific routes. we typically recommend an egress gateway pattern for strict allow-lists because it centralizes TLS inspection and FQDN allow-listing
01:30 Tomislav Novak: curious — are you talking about a managed proxy or a dedicated egress instance? we prefer not to have any public internet access from workers
01:38 Jonah Reyes: good question. for your use case we propose an internal egress gateway (customer-owned) that uses private endpoints to S3 and internal model stores. outbound to packages like OS updates or telemetry goes through the egress gateway which you lock down to the allowed destinations. workers have no direct NAT to the internet
01:56 Maya Patel: to add: we can also configure VPC endpoints for storage and control plane services so no traffic leaves the AWS backbone, and we support peering and transit gateway models for multi-account setups
02:12 Liam O'Connor: what about TLS certs and mTLS between components? we require mutual TLS for intra-service comms
02:20 Jonah Reyes: we support mTLS for service-to-service and TLS 1.2/1.3 for client traffic. we also support connecting to your CA for cert issuance, or we can use cert-manager in your cluster. the KV cache and model runtime can be locked behind mTLS and RBAC enforced at the control plane
02:38 Sana Ahmed: on keys — BYOK — can you integrate with our Thales HSM? we don't want cloud provider KMS holding keys in clear for critical models
02:45 Jonah Reyes: yes, we have patterns: either BYOK where customer keys are imported into supported cloud KMS with HSM-backed key material, or direct HSM integration via a key proxy. for on-prem we can run a key agent that forwards signing requests to your HSM without keys ever leaving the hardware security module
03:08 Dr. Emily Carter: how is key rotation audited? we need proof in SOC 2 reports of key lifecycle operations and role separation
03:16 Jonah Reyes: all KMS operations are logged — key usage, creation, rotation — propagate to CloudTrail (or equivalent). for BYOK with an HSM proxy, the proxy emits logs and we can forward events to your SIEM. we can supply an audit export showing timestamps and actor identities
03:33 Maya Patel: quick note — our SOC 2 pack contains samples of key lifecycle logs and RBAC change events. i'll share those in the artifacts bundle
03:40 Liam O'Connor: about audit logs, we need guaranteed write-once storage and tamper evidence. can Redwood push to our Splunk collector over TLS?
03:50 Jonah Reyes: yes, we support log shipping to customer SIEM via secure forwarders (TLS + client cert). we can also write logs to S3 with object-lock enabled for WORM retention and cross-account replication to your audit account
04:08 Sana Ahmed: for flow logs and VPC logging, we need 12 months retention and daily integrity checks. is that doable?
04:17 Jonah Reyes: straightforward — VPC Flow Logs to your logging account, retention policy and lifecycle rules set on the bucket. integrity checks via checksums and we can produce manifests for attestation
04:30 Tomislav Novak: wondering about egress DNS allow-lists. we have FQDN-level policies, not just IPs. some cloud providers' NAT won't do FQDN enforcement well
04:40 Jonah Reyes: right — that's why egress gateway + proxy is preferred. the proxy does SNI/FQDN inspection and allow-lists. we also support outbound filtering at L7 with Envoy if you want path-level controls
04:55 Liam O'Connor: can we run intrusion detection? we need visibility for east-west traffic inside the VPC too
05:02 Jonah Reyes: you can deploy IDS agents on subnets or mirror traffic to a collector; Redwood supports traffic mirroring to your inspection appliances. for private deployments we can integrate with your IDS/IPS with no outbound requirements
05:18 Maya Patel: shifting to RBAC and SSO — does your team need SAML integration details? we usually map Redwood roles to Okta groups and support SCIM for provisioning
05:27 Sana Ahmed: yes, SCIM and role mapping are required. also separation of duties: devs shouldn't be able to change egress ACLs or create keys
05:35 Jonah Reyes: we support fine-grained RBAC; ops roles are distinct from admin roles. we also have audit trails for role changes and can export role-change events for SOC evidence
05:48 Dr. Emily Carter: what about on-prem option — some of our compute needs to be air-gapped for PHI workloads; how does data residency work there?
05:59 Jonah Reyes: for air-gapped we offer an on-prem package where the control plane is a private console in your network (no public control plane). data endpoints and model weights stay within your network. we ship a hardened appliance or helm charts for bare-metal; connectivity to Redwood-managed services is optional
06:18 Tomislav Novak: any differences in egress handling on-prem vs cloud?
06:23 Jonah Reyes: on-prem you control all egress and ingress; Redwood's runtime runs as containers/VMs and respects your network policies. we provide recommended firewall rule sets and default-deny host-level policies. for updates we can provide air-gapped update bundles transferred via secure media
06:42 Maya Patel: i want to call out the shared responsibility model — Redwood can provide controls and defaults, but enforcement and network hardening within your VPC or data center is customer-managed unless you opt for our managed on-prem service
06:55 Liam O'Connor: ok backing up — for SOC 2 we need a list of artifacts to prove controls. what do you typically provide?
07:03 Maya Patel: we'll provide architecture diagrams, control mappings, sample logs (anonymized), key rotation logs, role-change logs, and test evidence for backups and retention. we'll also include our penetration test summary and hardening checklists
07:18 Dr. Emily Carter: good. on the networking diagram — i'd like to see explicit egress ACLs and which FQDNs your components call out to. sometimes vendor docs skip the small details
07:27 Jonah Reyes: understood. we'll annotate the diagram with egress destinations and call paths, and mark which are controllable via endpoints/peering and which require allow-lists
07:36 Sana Ahmed: about certificate pinning and mTLS again — how do you manage cert rotation across running workloads?
07:44 Jonah Reyes: cert-manager or our key agent can automate rotation and we publish rotation events into the audit log. for critical services we recommend short-lived certs with automated rolling to minimize blast radius
07:59 Tomislav Novak: storage access — do runtimes access S3 directly? I'm concerned about presigned URLs leaking to the internet
08:07 Jonah Reyes: we use VPC endpoints and IAM roles. presigned URLs are only generated within the VPC and service tokens are short-lived. additionally, you can require requests to originate from the egress gateway
08:20 Liam O'Connor: let's talk about fallback and graceful degradation — if the egress gateway fails, do workers fail closed? we cannot have silent fallback to direct internet
08:30 Jonah Reyes: yes we design fail-closed policies. the runtime will prefer private endpoints; if the egress gateway is unavailable requests are throttled/queued and we fail safe. for critical paths we have canary routes and multi-AZ redundancy for the egress gateway
08:46 Maya Patel: there's often a question about monitoring — what telemetry do you emit and where does it go?
08:51 Jonah Reyes: token-level metrics, per-route latency, KV cache hit/miss, and audit events. metrics can be pushed to Prometheus in your observability stack, while audit events go to CloudTrail or local syslog for SIEM ingestion
09:05 Sana Ahmed: retention policy again — SOC 2 wants 12 months for logs and 3 years for some artifacts. can you confirm Redwood can comply if logs are forwarded to our archive?
09:13 Maya Patel: yes, we can forward and we can also retain short-term copies to help with debugging but for compliance we recommend the canonical store be your archive with enforced retention
09:25 Dr. Emily Carter: one more about data-in-rest encryption — do you encrypt model weights and cache at rest? and who controls the master key?
09:34 Jonah Reyes: models and caches are encrypted at rest using KMS keys. in BYOK mode, you control the master key. in customer-managed KMS integration, Redwood never sees key material in plaintext
09:45 Liam O'Connor: any limitations on hardware HSM integration for latency-sensitive workloads? we run gen-inference with KV cache and need sub-10ms key ops ideally
09:55 Jonah Reyes: HSMs add latency; we suggest local key caching or wrapping strategies where the HSM signs ephemeral keys and the runtime uses symmetric keys for hot paths — this keeps critical operations sub-10ms while preserving auditability
10:13 Sana Ahmed: about proof of isolation — can you provide test steps we can run to validate there is no egress from worker subnets?
10:21 Jonah Reyes: yes, we'll provide a test plan: traffic emulation, egress-scan tests, DNS leak tests, and a CI job that verifies only expected FQDNs resolve and HTTP calls fail otherwise
10:33 Maya Patel: i'll capture that as an action item.
10:36 Tomislav Novak: anything around automated hardening? we run CIS benchmarks, do you have an automated compliance scan?
10:43 Jonah Reyes: we ship CIS-based hardening scripts and a compliance agent that reports compliance state back to your console. you can run periodic scans and pull a report for auditors
10:55 Liam O'Connor: question on network segmentation — do you recommend separate accounts per environment for least privilege?
11:03 Jonah Reyes: yes, multi-account or multi-project segmentation is best. we support cross-account peering and assume-role patterns for service accounts; transit gateway patterns tie everything together with explicit routing
11:18 Dr. Emily Carter: what does the onboarding timeline look like for a pilot? we want to ensure we can complete evidence collection for a SOC 2 readiness gap in 8 weeks
11:26 Maya Patel: typically pilot + initial hardening takes 2–4 weeks, then evidence collection and a remediation sprint can fit in the next 4 weeks. we can prioritize the SOC controls you need and produce artifacts quickly
11:38 Sana Ahmed: can you show a sample firewall rule set in the next deck?
11:43 Maya Patel: yes, jonah will draft a default deny set with explicit allow rules per component
11:48 Jonah Reyes: i'll include NAT vs egress gateway tradeoffs and an example Envoy L7 policy
11:53 Liam O'Connor: about escalation and incident response — if we detect a suspected exfiltration, what's the playbook with Redwood?
12:02 Maya Patel: we have an incident response SLA in the enterprise agreement. we'll coordinate with your triage team, provide diagnostic logs, and can support isolation of the affected nodes. we'll also supply post-mortem artifacts for auditors
12:17 Dr. Emily Carter: ok i'm comfortable with next steps. let's schedule the pilot kickoff and a follow-up SIEM integration deep dive
12:25 Maya Patel: agreed. we'll send calendar invites and the artifact bundle by Friday
12:30 Meeting close: thanks everyone

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-transcriptions of acronyms (e.g., 'KV cache' transcribed as 'K-V cash' in earlier auto-text), speaker overlap where Tomislav and Liam interject.
